title: Console-first runtime invocation showcase with AstraGrid
summary: Redwood team ran a console-forward walkthrough of JSON-mode, typed outputs, and safe-invoke flows. Customer was focused on private deployment, auditability (audit logs / KMS), and predictable latency for inference. Discussed pilot scope: 3-week gateway pilot, run perf benchmarks, security review. Action items: share security pack, pilot pricing, console recording and sample schema repo.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-22 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Product), Tom Ellis (CTO, AstraGrid), Maya Chen (ML Platform), Ravi Patel (Security), Lena Ortiz (Eng Manager)
---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, with jordan and priya. quick roll call?
[00:10] Tom: hey tom here, maya and ravi and lena on our side. excited to see the console-first flow you mentioned.
[00:16] Maya: yeah we want to validate a safe invoke path and how schemas prevent lateral actions.
[00:22] Jordan: great, today we'll show console demo of typed outputs, json-mode enforcement, then a runtime safe-invoke where the model calls a tool under guardrails. we'll also highlight routing, canaries and fallback policies.
[00:34] Priya: quick note on agenda - 1) live console walkthrough, 2) sample schema + sandboxed tool, 3) integration options (hosted / dedicated / private), 4) next steps + pilot.
[00:47] Tom: perfect. on our side, stack is mostly kubernetes on GCP, we run a model-serving infra (custom TF/torch) and have strict data residency needs for some pipelines. timeline is 6-8 weeks to evaluate. cost vs latency is a hard constraint.
[01:03] Jordan: noted. is there a preference for private deployment vs dedicated?
[01:10] Maya: we'd prefer private in a VPC or on-prem for PII workloads; for some product features we could use dedicated if isolation is sufficient.
[01:20] Ravi: and we need SOC2 plus support for our KMS, also audit logs and SAML/SSO for console.
[01:28] Alex: all supported — we'll share SOC2 docs and our KMS integration notes. the console ties into SSO via SAML, and audit logs can be exported.
[01:36] Jordan: jumping into the console: opening the JSON-mode playground...
[01:44] [screen share noises] Jordan: here you can define a response schema. i'm loading a sample schema for a ticket triage action — schema enforces fields like priority, assignee, and a safe_action boolean.
[02:02] Jordan: hitting run in strict mode — note the runtime enforces types and rejects malformed fields; we also have a fallback contract that maps to a text-only answer if typed output fails.
[02:18] Lena: does that fallback preserve intent or does it just return free-form?
[02:22] Jordan: the fallback returns a validated plain text fallback plus a confidence metric. you can configure automatic retrains or call a smaller deterministic model for structured responses.
[02:34] [02:40] Tom: walk me through how a tool call would work — we have a secure incident responder tool behind our VPC that we only want invoked after approval.
[02:48] Jordan: great question. we have a sandboxed tool execution flow: the model outputs a typed invocation, the runtime evaluates policy rules (RBAC, allowlist, rate limit), and then either routes to the tool or returns a dry-run response. for private deployment we can keep the tool adapter inside your VPC — the control plane can be customer-managed.
[03:10] Maya: pause — is the policy engine rule language shipped? how do we author rules for say only senior engineers or ciertos product lines?
[03:18] Priya: policy rules are authored in a YAML policy file in the console; you can map SAML groups to roles and create allowlists per tool. the console has a policy preview so you can simulate requests.
[03:30] Ravi: and audit trail? if someone triggers a tool we need an immutable log with request token and KV cache id.
[03:38] Jordan: yes we export audit logs with token-level metadata, model variant, KV cache reference, and the policy decision reason. these logs can be shipped to your SIEM or GCS.
[03:48] Tom: latency question — when we do a guarded tool call with policy check and internal VPC call, what's typical p95?
[03:56] Jordan: for private deployment on dedicated GPUs we've seen p95 around 120-220 ms for simple text gen. For a guarded invocation with a same-region tool call add 40-80ms network overhead in most cases; but we need to run a perf bench with your sequence lengths to be precise.
[04:15] Lena: do you support quantized model binaries for lower cost? we run a mix of mt-large models.
[04:21] Priya: yes, the runtime supports int8 and mixed-8 quantization profiles; the console Optimize tab suggests quant profiles per workload. you can pin a quantized variant for a route.
[04:31] Tom: how would batching affect latency? some of our flows are latency-sensitive, others can batch.
[04:36] Jordan: routing policies allow per-route batching windows and maximum delay. you'll see in console how routes are configured — you can set SLOs and the runtime will prioritize low-latency buckets and optionally drop into cheaper batched pools for best-effort requests.
[04:50] [05:00] Jordan: i'm going to demonstrate a safe-invoke: model produces an invocation JSON -> validate against schema -> policy evaluator does role allowlist check -> if allowed call tool adapter in VPC. I'll simulate a denied case first.
[05:12] [screen noise] Jordan: here's an invocation with action:"restart-service", target:{"service_id":"svc-12"}, requestor_group:"engineering:junior"
[05:24] system: policy evaluation: DENY (rule: restart-service requires role engineering:senior)
[05:28] Maya: nice, the deny reason is clear. can we customize error messages for the app to surface?
[05:33] Priya: yes, we let you map policy outcomes to structured responses and error codes so your front end can show localized messages.
[05:42] Tom: what about partial acceptance — e.g., model asks to escalate but we want a human approve step?
[05:47] Jordan: there's an approval flow. the runtime can persist a pending invocation in your queue and send an approval webhook to your approver. after approval the runtime replays the invocation and proceeds. all events are logged.
[05:58] Ravi: security — can we run the control plane in our VPC?
[06:02] Alex: yes, private deployment option supports a customer-controlled control plane that talks to runtime nodes via mutual TLS. we also offer an on-prem appliance for air-gapped deployments.
[06:10] Ravi: KMS integration? we need HSM-backed keys for model prompts that include PII.
[06:14] Priya: we integrate with major cloud KMS and HSM providers. for private deployments you can bring your own KMS and we store only ciphertext in logs.
[06:22] Tom: okay let's talk about a pilot — we want to exercise: 1) console JSON-mode policies, 2) safe-invoke to our internal ticket tool, 3) perf baseline for 3 endpoints. what's a realistic pilot timeline?
[06:33] Alex: a focused pilot is usually 2-4 weeks. recommended scope: week 0 provisioning and onboarding, week 1 schema and policy workshops, week 2 run perf + integration, week 3 validation and wrap. budget depends if you want dedicated vs private.
[06:47] Lena: what's the pricing cliff between dedicated and private for a pilot?
[06:52] Alex: we can do a short-term dedicated pilot with smaller commit; for private we'll propose a pilot license plus engineering onboarding. we'll share pricing options after this call.
[07:01] Tom: do you have any existing connectors for our ticketing system (we use Picket, LabsFlow)?
[07:06] Jordan: we have a webhook adapter and a sample integration repo. if you need a first-class connector we can scope a quick connector build in the pilot.
[07:14] [07:25] Maya: can we see an example schema you've used in production for a similar triage?
[07:29] Jordan: yes i'll open the schema library — here's a triage schema that enforces enums for priority, an assignee type, and disallows arbitrary exec fields. note sometimes transcriptions of fields get weird, we do keep stable contract names though.
[07:51] Tom: you mentioned KV cache earlier — will the cache leak context across tenants?
[07:55] Priya: caches are tenant-scoped; we never co-mingle KV state across customers. within Dedicated you can even pin cache isolation per-pool.
[08:04] Ravi: about compliance, do you support export controls or data residency for eu customers?
[08:09] Alex: yes, region pinning and data residency controls are supported. for sensitive regulated data we recommend Private with your regional infra.
[08:18] Lena: small thing — what's the developer experience for instrumenting cost per route?
[08:22] Priya: console shows token-level breakdown and per-route cost estimation; Optimize suggests batch/quantization changes and shows estimated delta.
[08:31] [08:40] Jordan: now i want to do a quick live demo of a structured fallback pattern — model returns incomplete fields, runtime tries a typed-correction pass against a micro-policy and either patches or marks as partial.
[08:53] [screen] Jordan: here's an incomplete output — missing assignee — the runtime runs a secondary parse and will place confidence<0.6 into partial field and surface a validation error to the application.
[09:06] Tom: can we set an automatic retry to a deterministic model?
[09:09] Jordan: yes you can define a fallback chain: main model -> structured correction model -> deterministic template model. all of this is visible in the console trace.
[09:19] Maya: what about tool calling safety when a model hallucinate a call — is there a way to require signed requests from the console?
[09:26] Priya: yes, tool adapters can require signed invocation tokens issued by the control plane. the runtime will only forward requests with a valid signature and policy pass. that prevents model-only arbitrary calls.
[09:35] Ravi: log retention — how long do you keep token-level logs?
[09:38] Alex: default is 90 days but enterprise plans can configure retention and export; for private you can control retention fully.
[09:46] [10:00] Jordan: switching to an example: i'll show a canary rollout rule where traffic to the new json-mode runtime is 10% and we have automatic regression rollback if error-rate > 2% or latency > 300ms.
[10:15] Jordan: in the console you can overlay token-level cost, latency, and quality metrics. you can also pin a dataset of prompts to run regression evals per-rollout.
[10:28] Tom: do you support local evals? we try to run in-house checks to avoid sending prompts externally.
[10:34] Priya: yes, you can run evals in your private deployment. the Console also supports local runners for offline evals.
[10:42] Lena: ok what about developer onboarding — how long for our engineers to be productive?
[10:46] Alex: most engineers can run basic console workflows in a day; integrating tool adapters + policies may take a sprint depending on complexity.
[10:54] [11:00] Tom: any competitive differentiators we should know — we're evaluating several vendors.
[11:04] Alex: we focus on production-grade runtime with baked-in typed outputs and guarded invocation. unlike some vendors that just give you model endpoints, we give orchestration, auditability, and guardrails plus private deployment options.
[11:18] Maya: do you have references that have implemented approval flows and private tool adapters?
[11:22] Alex: yes, we'll share a couple of references after the call.
[11:27] [11:40] Jordan: closing demo and moving to Q&A.
[11:44] Ravi: small technical: how are schema mismatches surfaced in logs? do you get the raw model output and the verified output?
[11:51] Jordan: logs include both the raw LM output (redacted if PII) and the validated typed output with diff highlights; you can configure redaction at field-level.
[12:02] Tom: about scaling — if we want 2000 qps for chat-style agents, how do you recommend architecture?
[12:09] Priya: you'd typically use a mix of Dedicated pools and autoscaled private runtime nodes with a routing policy that segments traffic by latency class. use prefix caching for repeated contexts to reduce cost.
[12:21] Lena: what SLA do you offer on dedicated?
[12:24] Alex: Standard SLA for Dedicated is 99.9% with latency targets per model class; enterprise plans can go higher.
[12:31] [12:40] Tom: ok next steps — we need: security pack, pilot price, sample schema repo, console recording. Also an internal tech deep-dive with our infra team.
[12:50] Alex: noted. we'll share SOC2, architecture diagram for private deployment, sample schema repo, and an initial pilot SOW.
[12:58] Maya: can you include a quick checklist for what we need to provision in our cloud project?
[13:03] Priya: yes we'll include a provisioning checklist and a perf benchmark template.
[13:09] Tom: tentative next meeting — tech deep dive on April 1st.
[13:13] Alex: we'll propose a few times and get it on calendar. thanks everyone.
---
Post-meeting notes (auto): we captured demo recording and console schema artifacts. customer strongly interested in private deployment for PII flows. pilot requested: 3-week scoped pilot covering console policies, safe-invoke integration, and perf baseline.
